The lighthouse keeper climbed the spiral staircase every evening at dusk to light the great lamp and check the oil reserves, then he wrote the weather observations in the logbook with precise care, noting the wind direction, the sea state, and the visibility of the distant ships on the horizon. He trimmed the wick, polished the glass panels, and adjusted the rotation mechanism so the beam swept the same four sectors it had swept for generations, a steady rhythm that the fishing fleets relied on to round the headland safely even when the fog rolled in thick from the north.

The wind outside had shifted, carrying the salt-heavy bite of an approaching storm. He paused at the top of the stairs, his hand resting on the cold iron railing, and listened. The usual hum of the mechanism was steady, but beneath it, he could hear the low groan of the tower settling against the gale. It was a sound he had known for thirty years, a lullaby of stone and steel.

He turned back to the logbook, his pen hovering over the page. *Wind: NW, 35 knots. Sea: Rough. Visibility: Poor.* He added one more line, a private note that no one else would ever read: *The light holds. The keeper holds.*

Then, he descended the stairs, one step at a time, ready to face the night.
